results.title: Dangerous and Reckless Message of Using Extrajudicial Killings as a Shield for Failure to Maintain Law and Order; TIB Calls for Withdrawal of IGP’s Remarks and Accountability
results.content:
**Press Release**

**Dhaka, 26 October 2026:** Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has strongly condemned and expressed deep concern over the Inspector General of Police’s (IGP) remarks that the police would resort to crossfire, if necessary, to maintain law and order, provided the government gives its approval. According to TIB, the remarks send a dangerous message by presenting extrajudicial killings as an acceptable means of crime control, rather than addressing failures in maintaining law and order and institutional weaknesses. Describing the remarks as an expression of utter disregard for the Constitution and the rule of law, TIB has demanded their immediate withdrawal, accountability of the IGP, and accountability for making a declaration that contradicts the government’s stated position against extrajudicial killings.

TIB Executive Director Dr. Iftekharuzzaman said, “Is the police chief seeking to use the discredited practice of crossfire as a shield for the police’s failure to maintain law and order? Does seeking to legitimise extrajudicial killings by making them conditional on government approval amount to an admission of failure to combat crime through lawful means? The responsibility of the police is to conduct professional investigations, identify offenders and bring the accused to trial on the basis of admissible evidence. Presenting crossfire as an alternative cannot resolve institutional weaknesses; rather, it is an example of professional bankruptcy. In the same remarks, the IGP spoke of discharging duties in accordance with the law and the Constitution, while also saying that the police would resort to crossfire if the government approved it. These two positions are contradictory. No government approval can legitimise an extrajudicial killing. The rights to legal protection and to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution cannot be set aside by executive decisions. Regardless of the seriousness of an allegation, the police have no authority to kill anyone by bypassing due process.”

Recalling past experiences, the TIB Executive Director said, “The conviction of police officers in the Sinha murder case, along with allegations reported in connection with the verdict that crossfire was used to extort money, torture people and kill them, serves as a reminder of the horrific nature of this practice. The killing of Teknaf municipal councillor Ekramul Haque in a purported gunfight also raised serious questions, particularly following the release of an audio recording by his family and allegations of murder. The convictions of former RAB officials in the Narayanganj seven-murder case provide another judicially established example of the criminal abuse of power by law enforcement agencies. Despite thousands of such experiences, and amid public expectations for police reform and broader state reform, the police chief is once again raising the prospect of crossfire. He must answer the question of what lessons the police have learned from past crimes.”

Dr. Zaman further said, “Such reckless and ill-considered remarks by the police chief could be perceived as an implicit licence for unlawful use of force at the field level. When the person responsible for ensuring that the force operates within the law presents crossfire as an alternative, questions about his sense of responsibility and suitability for leadership inevitably arise. How can the public trust that, under his leadership, citizens’ lives and legal protections will be safeguarded? On the other hand, on 14 September, the Law Minister stated that the government would not resort to crossfire to combat terrorism and that existing laws were sufficient to tackle terrorism. Why, then, is the police chief raising the prospect of crossfire subject to government approval? The government must clearly explain this inconsistency and specify how accountability will be ensured for implementing its declared position.”

TIB said that any use of force by the police must be lawful, necessary and proportionate. Under international standards, the intentional lethal use of firearms is permissible only when strictly unavoidable to protect life. There is no scope to portray this narrowly defined exception as authorisation for extrajudicial killings. Regarding allegations that journalists criticise the police because they have not received money, TIB said that if there are specific allegations of criminal conduct against any journalist, lawful action must be taken on the basis of evidence. Sweeping allegations undermine the role of a free media in oversight and accountability and risk discouraging independent journalism. The need to ensure a conducive working environment and adequate capacity for the police cannot be used as a justification for evading legitimate criticism.

TIB has called on the government to obtain a formal explanation of the IGP’s remarks, ensure their withdrawal along with an unconditional public apology, and hold him administratively accountable. The organisation has also called for his removal from office until accountability is ensured.

results.title: IGP’s ‘crossfire’ remarks do not reflect govt position: Home minister
results.content:
# IGP’s ‘crossfire’ remarks do not reflect govt position: Home minister

Salahuddin Ahmed says government firmly opposes extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and custodial deaths

 Published : 27 October 2026

•
 Updated : 27 October 2026, 19:08

• [ NEWS ](/news)

![Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed.png](/sites/default/files/styles/big_1/public/2026-10/Home%20Minister%20Salahuddin%20Ahmed.png?h=c673cd1c)

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed today told The Daily Star that the police chief’s remarks about conducting “crossfire” with government permission did not represent the government’s position.

The government was firmly opposed to extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and custodial deaths, he said.

Ahmed said the July mass uprising, which toppled the Awami League government in August 2024, had taken place to establish the rule of law. Upholding this principle is the government’s commitment to the people, he added.

Yesterday, Inspector General of Police Md Ali Hossain Fakir said at a programme in Dhaka’s Chawkbazar, “Wherever crossfire is necessary, if the government allows it, we will do that.”

Police Headquarters subsequently clarified that the IGP had not intended to endorse extrajudicial killings or punishment outside the judicial process. It said he was referring to firm action against criminals within the law.

The Bangladesh Police Service Association also issued a statement, saying the IGP’s comments should be understood in the context of existing laws and regulations.

The association described his remarks as a timely call for firm and uncompromising enforcement of the law. It said officers should be able to exercise their lawful powers, including the right of private defence, without unnecessary hesitation.

The association said police personnel had faced 176 attacks so far this year, leaving four officers dead and 370 seriously injured.

The statement did not address the IGP’s reference to government permission.

Under Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution, no person can be deprived of life except in accordance with law. The government has no authority to permit extrajudicial killings in the name of “crossfire”.

Bangladesh has a long history of deaths described by law enforcement agencies as “crossfire” or “gunfights”.

The practice became widespread after the BNP-led government established the Rapid Action Battalion (Rab) in 2004. Such killings continued under the military-backed caretaker administration in 2007-08 and the Awami League government from 2009 to 2024.

According to Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), 2,957 people were killed in alleged crossfire or gunfights involving law enforcement agencies between 2004 and September 2026.

The BNP’s 31-point state reform programme pledges to end enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings and bring those responsible for killings in the name of crossfire to justice.

results.title: Parties condemn attack on CPB headquarters, demand arrests
results.content:
# Parties condemn attack on CPB headquarters, demand arrests

## Leaders defend “Joy Bangla” as a historic Liberation War slogan belonging to no single party

[ ![Parties condemn attack on CPB headquarters, demand arrests](https://media.assettype.com/bdnews24-english/2026-10-27/3xr49bv6/basod_protest_271026.jpg?w=1024) ](https://media.assettype.com/bdnews24-english/2026-10-27/3xr49bv6/basod_protest_271026.jpg)

Published : 27 Oct 2026, 08:26 PM

Updated : 27 Oct 2026, 08:26 PM

Several political parties have condemned Monday night’s attack on the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) headquarters in Purana Paltan and demanded the arrest and trial of those involved.

The left-wing alliance Ganatantrik Jukto Front held a protest rally and procession outside the National Press Club on Tuesday.

Participants included Bangladesh Socialist Party (BaSaD) General Secretary Bazlur Rashid Firoz, CPB General Secretary Abdullah Al Kafi Ratan and Ganatantrik Biplobi Party General Secretary Mosharrefa Mishu.

Activists from the Bangladesh Students’ Union and Jubo Union alleged that local BNP, Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal members carried out the attack over claims of CPB links to the Awami League, whose activities are banned.

Police said tensions arose between CPB activists and members of the BNP and Jubo Dal over the slogan “Joy Bangla”.

In a statement, the CPB said a group carrying sticks gathered outside Mukti Bhaban at 10pm on Monday, claiming that members of a “banned party” were inside.

The group attempted to break through the main gate and several people were injured when CPB activists tried to stop them, the party said.

It added that the office remained blockaded even after police arrived.

Prime Minister’s Information Advisor Zahed Ur Rahman assured reporters at the Secretariat on Tuesday that the government would take action over the incident and similar offences.

Revolutionary Workers Party General Secretary Saiful Haque said violence and intimidation against people holding different political views threatened democracy.

He urged the government to prevent such incidents from recurring.

Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal President ASM Abdur Rab and General Secretary Shahid Uddin Mahmud Swapan also condemned the incident and the reported obstruction of the burial of freedom fighter Manik Pashari in Pirojpur.

They said “Joy Bangla” was a historic Liberation War slogan, not the property of any single political party, and condemned its use as a pretext for violence.

In a joint statement, Ganoshanghati Andolon acting Chief Coordinator Dewan Abdur Rashid Nilu and Executive Coordinator Abul Hasan Rubel called for an investigation, legal action against those involved and security for political party offices and activists.

results.title: As salaries run out in 20 days, people turn to borrowing
results.content:
## For many salaried employees in Dhaka, the money runs out almost ten days before the month does. Inflation and rising prices leave them with little or no savings, pushing them into a vicious cycle of borrowing to get by

**Anas Ahmed works for a private company and earns Tk54,000 a month. He lives with his family and pays Tk20,000 in rent. Gas cylinders, water and electricity cost another Tk5,000, while installments for an iPhone he bought six months ago take up Tk5,500.**

Because the metro does not serve his route to work, Anas usually travels by motorcycle, spending Tk7,000–Tk8,000 a month on fuel and transport. Groceries cost another Tk5,000–Tk7,000.

These expenses alone account for up to Tk45,000 of his salary, leaving a little for other family needs and unexpected costs.

Anas tries to save Tk5,000 a month, but regular expenses often force him to use that money. By the 25th, he is frequently out of cash. He sometimes borrows Tk5,000–Tk10,000 through a mobile financial service to get through the remaining days. The three-month loans carry interest, and repaying them from his next salary puts further pressure on his budget.

"Costs rise every day, but salaries do not," he said. "The company may give us a yearly pay rise of Tk2,000 to Tk4,000. But that does not keep up with rising costs."

Niloy, who also works for a private company, echoes the same concerns. "Costs are rising so fast that I have to think about earning extra money alongside my job," he said. "But I struggle to find the time or the chance to do so."

Anas and Niloy are not alone in facing these challenges. Rising living costs make it harder for many salaried employees in Dhaka to save, forcing some to borrow money to cover their expenses.

The country's inflation figures show how prices continue to rise. Data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) show that overall inflation stood at 8.34% in September 2026, up from 8.26% in August. Food inflation rose from 7.02% to 7.22%, while non-food inflation edged down from 9.32% to 9.3%.

Average inflation over the 12 months to September 2026 was 8.65%, compared with 9.45% in the preceding 12 months. A falling inflation rate does not necessarily mean falling prices, it means prices are rising more slowly. Households therefore continue paying more for goods and services than they did before.

Mahtab Uddin, assistant professor of Economics at the University of Dhaka and Honorary Research Director at the South Asian Network on Economic Modelling (SANEM), believes Bangladesh's inflation problem must be understood in the context of its monetary and fiscal policy decisions.

"While countries such as Britain and India raised interest rates to contain inflation, Bangladesh failed to tighten monetary policy sufficiently or at the right time," he said. "Continued liquidity support for distressed banks and expansionary fiscal policy added to inflationary pressures."

Bangladesh's weak tax collection and substantial expenditure on large development projects also contributed to fiscal pressure, according to Mahtab. These structural factors made it harder to control inflation even as households struggled with rising prices.

**When households are forced to cut back**

The consequences are particularly severe for lower-income households, which spend a larger share of their earnings on necessities.

"When prices rise and real wages fail to keep pace, people are forced to make difficult choices," Mahtab said, "Families may stop buying fish, meat or fruit, switch to less nutritious food or reduce spending on their children's education."

Such adjustments can have consequences beyond the monthly budget, affecting nutrition, education and long-term economic mobility. For households already struggling to cover essentials, there may be little discretionary spending left to cut.

The pressure also depends on how much a family spends on essentials such as food, rent and transport. When these costs absorb most of its income, there is little left for savings or unexpected expenses.

Wages have also struggled to keep pace with prices. According to the BBS Wage Rate Index, national wage growth was 7.9% in September 2026, below overall inflation of 8.34%. The gap was 0.44 percentage points.

> In Britain, teachers, doctors and railway workers have used organised action to demand better pay. In Bangladesh, many workers, including white-collar employees, lack similar bargaining power. When labour supply exceeds demand, negotiating pay rises that keep pace with living costs becomes even harder.

The figures do not mean every worker has lost purchasing power, as individual pay rises and household spending patterns differ. But they indicate that, on average, wages have not kept up with rising prices, making it harder for many households to improve their financial position.

**The vicious cycle of borrowing**

The problem extends beyond salaried workers. Students who depend on family support also face pressure from transport and daily expenses.

Abdullah Al Mahmud, a private university student, spends at least Tk200 a day on fuel for his motorcycle commute. A round trip by metro costs Tk240, leaving him to weigh the costs before deciding how to travel.

Mahmud often hears friends say they borrow money towards the end of the month and repay it once their salaries arrive, leaving them short again the following month and forcing them to borrow again.

Mahtab argued that weak collective bargaining also limits workers' ability to negotiate higher wages.

"In Britain, teachers, doctors and railway workers have used organised action to demand better pay. In Bangladesh, many workers, including white-collar employees, lack similar bargaining power. When labour supply exceeds demand, negotiating pay rises that keep pace with living costs becomes even harder," he noted.

Not every budget shortfall comes from rent or other major bills. A hangout at restaurants, regular travel, online shopping and small discretionary purchases can also add up. Spending Tk100 a day without tracking it amounts to Tk3,000 over a month.

But cutting unnecessary expenses is only part of the solution. For a large number of people, the bigger challenge is finding ways to increase their income in an economy where suitable jobs remain scarce.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its October 2026 issue of Regional Economic Outlook for Asia and the Pacific, reported that nearly 29% of highly educated young people in Bangladesh are unemployed. The report also warned that AI could exert downward pressure equivalent to 2% of aggregate labour demand in Bangladesh.

These challenges point to a broader problem. While rising living costs, limited job opportunities and potential changes in labour demand could make it harder for people to improve their financial situation.

**Budgeting: One piece of the puzzle**

Mumitul Mimma, a journalist in Dhaka, says recording her expenses helped her understand where her money was going.

"I used to spend carelessly and struggle by mid-month. So I started keeping a spending diary, recording everything from transport fares to cups of tea. It helped me track where my money went and plan my spending better."

Tracking expenses can help people identify unnecessary spending and plan their budgets more realistically. But it does not solve the economic problem. People who spend almost all their income on food, housing, healthcare and family needs may have little room to cut costs.

This is where money management or personal finance comes as a crucial skill.

Setting aside money as soon as a salary arrives makes saving easier than waiting until month-end. A separate savings account, automatic transfer or monthly deposit scheme can help build the habit. Tracking expenses and keeping an emergency fund can also reduce the need to borrow.

"Whatever the cost of living, managing within your income takes skill. Even with today's high prices, many people are getting by on much less than you earn," said Manjura Akter, a teacher at Mohammadpur Government High School.

She recommends saving from the beginning of the month and planning expenditure around essential needs. A monthly savings scheme, such as a deposit pension scheme (DPS), may help people build discipline, while an emergency reserve can reduce pressure when unexpected costs arise.

However, budgeting has its limits. When income is insufficient to cover basic expenses, saving may simply be impossible. For households already struggling with rent, food and transport, the challenge is not only how to manage their money, but also whether their income can keep pace with the cost of living.
